newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals -- Lead seen sinking further, bouncing.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals -- Lead seen sinking further, bouncing.

text.p: Japanese traders said they expect further downward moves in the lead price after Friday's slide to 8-1/2-month lows, although some said the market could bounce with the approach of winter, the peak season for demand from the car battery sector.
On Friday LME benchmark three-month lead slid to $715 a tonne, its lowest level since late January and down nearly 15 percent from its mid-August highs.
"It certainly would not be odd for three-month lead (on the London Metal Exchange) to fall to $700 a tonne," said a trader at a large Japanese trade house.
He added that while a slip below $700 was also not out of the question, he expected the price would rebound to $750 by the end of the year.

Traders noted talk of stepped-up Chinese supply weighing on the market, although they viewed the recent declines largely as a correction of a rally that started late last year and peaked in early May at a 5-1/2-year high of $861 a tonne.

Estimates released last week by the International Lead and Zinc Study Group also pointed to a surplus of refined lead in 1997, with supplies forecast at 5.92 million tonnes and demand seen at 5.86 million tonnes.

Japanese traders doubted the recent slide in prices would spur any Japanese buying interest and noted high premiums on imports of $100 per tonne or more over LME cash prices and the offsetting effect of the falling yen.
"At premiums of $80 to $100, lead won't sell in Japan. There's nobody who'll buy it," said one trader, who added that many users' needs were already met through long-term contracts.

Flat demand and increased recycling of domestic scrap by Japan's refiners have also put a damper on Japanese lead imports, which tumbled in the first eight months of this year to 27,023 tonnes from 68,725 tonnes in the year-ago period.
Copper traders said there was little activity in the spot market, although domestic supplies remained relatively tight.
They saw little reason for worry about a recent accident at Chile's El Abra facility only two months after it produced its first refined copper.

Aluminium traders said end users were still in no hurry to buy, with the recent slide in prices on the LME partially offset by the weak yen. LME benchmark three-month aluminium prices hit a 2-1/2-year low of $1,305 a tonne on October 10, but have since clawed their way back above $1,350.
Japanese premiums rose modestly, however, reflecting higher premiums in the U.S. Midwest, traders said.
